title: Which build fits the card you own
music_mood: low and steady, no melody, one sustained tone that never argues with the numbers

scenes.narration: Twenty-seven billion parameters, in a file of six point one nine gigabytes. That is the smallest published build of one Qwen model, sitting on Unsloth's file table. You own one graphics card. You want to know what actually runs on it.
scenes.visual_intent: The episode's name and its series tag: this is a buyer's guide about which build to download, not a news item.

data.title: Which build fits the card you own

scenes.narration: Start with the honest part. Nothing in this episode was measured by us. The DGX Spark here was unreachable from the machine that makes these videos. Every number you hear carries the name of whoever published it. You can go and check each one.
scenes.visual_intent: A plain card admitting that no number in this episode was measured on this channel's own hardware.
on_screen_text: Not measured here. Every source named.

data.text: Nothing in this episode was measured by us. Every number carries the name of whoever published it.

scenes.narration: The model page hands you a parameter count. That number tells you almost nothing about whether the thing will load. What decides is how many gigabytes sit resident on your card while it runs. Only one of those numbers is printed where you are looking. The other one you have to go and find.
scenes.visual_intent: A parameter count is the number you are shown; gigabytes resident is the number that decides, and it is printed somewhere else.
on_screen_text: The model page hands you a parameter count
That number tells you almost nothing
What decides is how many gigabytes sit resident
Only one of those numbers is printed

scenes.narration: The decision in front of you is narrower than the argument people have online. You are picking a build. One model ships many builds of itself, and their file sizes sit nowhere near each other. That gap is where tonight's decision lives.
scenes.visual_intent: One model name fans out into several differently sized builds; the decision is which build, not which model.

scenes.narration: Say you own one consumer card, and you want the whole model resident on it. No second card. No renting time on a server somewhere. Whatever your card holds tonight, that number does not move, so everything else has to.
scenes.visual_intent: One card's memory, drawn once and fixed: no second card, no rented server, so everything else has to move instead.

scenes.narration: So build one small habit. Open the files listing on the model's repository and read the size of the build you want. Unsloth publishes exactly that table for the Qwen model, in gigabytes, beside every file name. That size is where the arithmetic starts.
scenes.visual_intent: A published file listing with sizes in gigabytes and the publisher's name in frame; that size is where the arithmetic starts.

scenes.narration: So is the file size the answer? Close. The file holds the weights, and it is the part you download. Three things share your card's memory once the model runs, and the file is only one of them.
scenes.visual_intent: Chapter two opens: the file is only one of the three things sharing the card's memory.

scenes.narration: Your own conversation is the cost people forget. Your model keeps running notes on every word so far. That is a KV cache, and it sits in the same memory as the weights. It starts small. It grows with every word you send and every word that comes back.
scenes.visual_intent: The weights sit still while a second block, the KV cache, grows with every word sent and every word returned.

scenes.narration: Think of the loaded weights as one room that never changes size. Your conversation keeps a desk in that room, and the desk grows all evening. Desks do not shrink, and the room does not stretch to help.
scenes.visual_intent: A room that never changes size with a desk inside it that keeps growing; the room does not stretch to help.
on_screen_text: Think of the loaded weights as one room
Your conversation keeps a desk in that room
the room does not stretch to help

scenes.narration: NVIDIA publishes the arithmetic for that cache. Two, times the layers, times the heads, times the head dimension, times the bytes per value. That is the cost of one token, and NVIDIA works the example through itself.
scenes.visual_intent: NVIDIA's per-token cache cost written as words multiplied by words, not as symbols.
on_screen_text: NVIDIA publishes the arithmetic for that cache
That is the cost of one token

scenes.narration: Its worked example is Llama two at seven billion parameters. At a context of four thousand and ninety-six tokens, that arithmetic lands at roughly two gigabytes of cache. On a card holding eight gigabytes of memory, two gigabytes is not a rounding error.
scenes.visual_intent: Two gigabytes of cache, from NVIDIA's own worked example, taking a visible bite out of an eight gigabyte card.

data.caption: KV cache, Llama 2 7B at a 4,096 token context
data.context: NVIDIA's own worked example, not a rounding error on an 8 GB card

scenes.narration: Now, the formula as printed counts attention heads, which was right for the models of its day. Modern ones share those notes between groups of heads. Qwen's eight billion parameter model lists thirty-two query heads against eight key-value heads.
scenes.visual_intent: Thirty-two query heads collapse into eight shared key-value groups; the printed formula still counts the thirty-two.

scenes.narration: That sharing is grouped-query attention, and it cuts the notes several times over. Run the printed formula on a model built that way and you overstate its cache by four times. Those head counts come from the config file on Qwen's own repository.
scenes.visual_intent: Grouped-query attention cuts the cache several times over, so the printed formula overstates a modern model fourfold.
on_screen_text: it cuts the notes several times over
you overstate its cache by 4 times

scenes.narration: One cost is left, and nobody publishes it. A llama dot cpp maintainer says there is no easy way to calculate the context size. The same post notes the graphics runtime takes memory that may not be accounted for anywhere.
scenes.visual_intent: A maintainer's own sentence: the last cost has no easy calculation, so the band at the top of the bar gets no number.

data.text: There is no easy way to calculate the context size.

scenes.narration: That warning turns up in Ollama's documentation too, put the other way round. Set a longer context length and the memory required goes up. So the context window you type is a purchase, and you pay for it out of this same card.
scenes.visual_intent: The context length you type is a purchase: set it longer and the memory required goes up, paid out of the same card.

scenes.narration: So here is the one sum you can hold in your head. File size, plus cache for the context you actually run, subtracted from the memory on your card. Whatever is left, leave some of it alone. The runtime lives there.
scenes.visual_intent: The finished bar: file, cache and a top band that still carries no number, with slack deliberately left over.

scenes.narration: That sum has one dial you can turn. Quantization, storing each of the model's numbers with fewer bits, shrinks the file you download. Same model, same parameter count, smaller file. Every build on a repository page is one setting of that dial.
scenes.visual_intent: Chapter three opens: one dial, quantization, turns the same parameter count into different file sizes.

scenes.narration: Unsloth's table for that twenty-seven billion parameter Qwen model starts at six point one nine gigabytes. That is its bottom rung. The top rung is twenty-five point three gigabytes. Same weights, same parameter count, and one model that reaches every consumer card tier.
scenes.visual_intent: One model's published ladder, bottom rung to top rung, for the same twenty-seven billion parameters.

scenes.narration: That range is the whole point. An eight gigabyte card and a twenty-four gigabyte card can both run this model. They run different builds of it, and the distance between those builds is quality you agreed to give up.
scenes.visual_intent: The ladder's rungs line up against consumer card tiers: one model reaches all of them, as different builds.

data.title: Card tiers the same model reaches

scenes.narration: You can do this sum yourself, and it will mislead you. Twenty-seven billion parameters at four bits each comes to about thirteen and a half gigabytes. That is the number a lot of people trust. The published file table does not agree with it.
scenes.visual_intent: The viewer's own parameters-times-bits sum appears, then the published file table refuses to agree with it.
on_screen_text: You can do this sum yourself
The published file table does not agree

scenes.narration: The label is not the width. On llama dot cpp's own quantize table, Q four K M measures four point eight nine bits per weight. Q eight zero measures eight point five bits per weight. Each block of numbers carries a scale on top of its payload bits.
scenes.visual_intent: Nominal quantization labels sit beside their measured widths, and none of them line up.

scenes.narration: Every rung down that ladder has a published price. llama dot cpp measures it with perplexity, which is how surprised a model is by ordinary text. Lower is better. Their table runs the comparison at seven billion parameters.
scenes.visual_intent: The episode's table gains its quality column, measured in perplexity, and the column is still empty.

scenes.narration: At that size, Q four K M costs about plus zero point zero five perplexity. Q two K costs about plus zero point eight seven perplexity. Both of those sit on the same ladder, and they are nowhere near the same distance from the original.
scenes.visual_intent: Two published perplexity penalties side by side: one barely visible, one long.

scenes.narration: So spending your budget on parameters works, down to a point. Take the largest build whose file plus cache still fits, and stop before the bottom rungs. That is the rule most people run, and for plenty of work it is fine.
scenes.visual_intent: Row A fills across every column: take the largest build that fits, and stop before the bottom rungs.
on_screen_text: Row A: biggest model that fits

scenes.narration: Now turn that dial the other way. Take a smaller model and spend the same gigabytes on precision instead. The comparison table keeps its six columns and its units. Only the row underneath changes.
scenes.visual_intent: Chapter four opens: same axis, same units, a second row underneath the first.

scenes.narration: Ornith's nine billion parameter model publishes a four-bit build at five point six three gigabytes. Its eight-bit build is nine point five three gigabytes. So the entire ladder, all the way up to eight-bit, stays under ten gigabytes.
scenes.visual_intent: A short ladder whose top rung, the eight-bit build, still sits below the ten gigabyte line.

scenes.narration: That changes the question you are asking. The top of that ladder fits a twelve gigabyte card with room to spare. You are no longer deciding whether it runs. You are deciding how much of the original model you keep. That is a better question to be stuck on.
scenes.visual_intent: The whole ladder drops inside a twelve gigabyte card with space left over, so the question changes from whether to how much.

scenes.narration: Now the rule everyone repeats does have a source, and the source is a good one. A twenty twenty-two paper from Dettmers and Zettlemoyer concluded that four-bit precision is almost universally optimal. That is where bigger model, fewer bits comes from.
scenes.visual_intent: The sentence everyone quotes, with the paper and the year that produced it.

scenes.narration: Read what the paper says it measured. Zero-shot accuracy, which means answering questions with no worked examples given first. No instruction-tuned models in the sweep. No reasoning evaluation of any kind. The paper states that scope itself.
scenes.visual_intent: The paper's own stated scope, line by line, each one narrowing what the quoted sentence covers.
on_screen_text: Read what the paper says it measured
Zero-shot accuracy, no worked examples first
No instruction-tuned models in the sweep
No reasoning evaluation of any kind

scenes.narration: The sizes it tested ran from nineteen million parameters up to a hundred and seventy-six billion of them. Every model in it was released before twenty twenty-two. The paper is careful about all of this. The people quoting it usually are not.
scenes.visual_intent: The sizes the sweep covered, and the date stamp that greys the whole source out.
on_screen_text: The sizes it tested ran from 19M parameters
Every model in it was released before 2022
The people quoting it usually are not

scenes.narration: Then there is what happened to the models themselves. The Scaling Laws for Precision paper measured degradation under quantization, and it increases with training data size. That held across every model size they tested. So a model trained on more tokens has more to lose when you shrink it.
scenes.visual_intent: More training tokens on one side, more damage under quantization on the other; the arrow between them is the finding.

scenes.narration: A twenty twenty-five controlled study went at reasoning directly, across roughly seventeen hundred inference scenarios. An eight billion parameter model at eight-bit consistently beat a fourteen billion parameter model at four-bit. That is the rule running backwards.
scenes.visual_intent: The size of the controlled reasoning study, and the result that runs the rule backwards.

scenes.narration: The same study goes further. A thirty-two billion parameter model at four-bit was strictly dominated by both of the others. On reasoning work, bigger and blurrier lost to smaller and sharper. Nothing about that ordering follows from the parameter count.
scenes.visual_intent: Three builds ranked on reasoning: the largest one, at four bits, sits lowest of the three.

scenes.narration: So when two builds both fit your card, the parameter count stops being the tiebreak. Ask what you are running the model for. If the answer is reasoning, the measured order says take the smaller model at higher precision.
scenes.visual_intent: Row B fills across the same columns and the quality cell is the only one that flips which row reads better.

scenes.narration: Long documents pull that gap wider than reasoning does. A twenty twenty-five study went at long-context tasks. Eight-bit held accuracy there to about a zero point eight percent drop. Four-bit methods lost up to fifty-nine percent of their accuracy.
scenes.visual_intent: Chapter five opens: the gap is widest on long documents, which is where the exceptions start.

scenes.narration: A loss of that size is not a quality nudge. That is a model going soft on the exact job you bought the memory for. Long context and cheap builds are a bad pairing.
scenes.visual_intent: The table again, with one row ringed: long context and cheap builds are a bad pairing.

data.title: Long context changes the quality cell

scenes.narration: Three situations should ignore everything so far. Start with a mixture of experts. That is a model split into specialists, with a router that wakes a few per word. Every expert stays resident in memory anyway.
scenes.visual_intent: A router wakes a few experts per word while every expert stays resident in memory anyway.

scenes.narration: Hugging Face writes it plainly. Mixtral needs enough memory for a dense forty-seven billion parameter model. It computes at the speed of a twelve billion parameter one. You pay memory for every expert and get the speed of a few.
scenes.visual_intent: You pay memory for a dense forty-seven billion parameter model and get the compute of a twelve billion one.

scenes.narration: Some models are not a fitting question at all. Unsloth's smallest published build of DeepSeek V four Flash is eighty-two and a half gigabytes. That is more than three times a twenty-four gigabyte card. No build on that page gets you there.
scenes.visual_intent: One file block dwarfing the memory bar it was meant to sit inside; no build on that page gets you there.

data.caption: smallest published build of DeepSeek V4 Flash (Unsloth)
data.context: more than three times a 24 GB card

scenes.narration: And your runtime may never tell you it went wrong. Ollama does not refuse a model that will not fit. It splits the layers between your card and your processor, and it keeps answering questions.
scenes.visual_intent: Layers spilling out of the card into system memory while the runtime keeps answering and never says a word about it.
on_screen_text: it splits, it does not refuse

scenes.narration: Ollama's documentation shows the shape of that. The process listing prints the split. It shows values such as forty-eight percent on the processor against fifty-two percent on the card. llama dot cpp's own guide calls that arrangement, in its words, much slower.
scenes.visual_intent: The shape of the process listing Ollama documents, typed out, with the split percentages in the processor column; not a recording of our own run.
on_screen_text: shape of the documented output, not a capture

data.title: ollama ps, shape of Ollama's documented output
data.code:
$ ollama ps
NAME    ID    SIZE    PROCESSOR            UNTIL
...     ...   ...     48%/52% CPU/GPU      ...

scenes.narration: And nobody publishes the number you would need to do this exactly. The runtime takes its slice, and no source found for this episode puts a figure on it. So leave the top of the card alone. Do not fill it to the brim.
scenes.visual_intent: The unlabelled band from chapter two, still carrying no number, with the instruction not to fill the card to the brim.

scenes.narration: So here is tonight's check. Load the model you were going to run anyway, then ask Ollama for its process listing. If it prints a split, part of your model is on the processor and you are paying for it.
scenes.visual_intent: The one check to run tonight, typed out: load the model, then ask for the process listing and read the split.

data.title: tonight's check
data.code:
# load the model you were going to run anyway
ollama run <your-model>

# then, in another shell, ask for the process listing
ollama ps

scenes.narration: Take the biggest model whose file plus cache still leaves your card room to spare. If the job is reasoning or long context, spend that room on bits, not parameters.
scenes.visual_intent: The channel wordmark and what comes next; the decision rule is the last thing spoken and nothing follows it.
